source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
“Where I Lived, and What I Lived For”

source.excerpt: Our life is frittered away by detail. An honest man has hardly need to count more than his ten fingers, or in extreme cases he may add his ten toes, and lump the rest. Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand; instead of a million count half a dozen, and keep your accounts on your thumb nail.
trail: The line appears verbatim in the first-edition text of Walden (1854), “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For” ↗.
The full text is also mirrored at Project Gutenberg’s edition of Walden ↗, where the passage reads identically.
Walden was first published by Ticknor and Fields in Boston in 1854, placing it firmly in the public domain in the United States.
The neighboring imperative “Simplify, simplify” comes a few sentences later in the same paragraph ↗ and is often quoted alongside or in place of this line.
source.excerptNote: The line is the climax of Thoreau’s argument for stripping life down to essentials; the same paragraph continues with the famous injunction “Simplify, simplify.”
source.rightsNote: Walden was first published in 1854, so both the work and this passage have long been in the public domain in the United States; the original text is freely reproducible.

author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, poet, and naturalist associated with New England Transcendentalism. From 1845 to 1847 he lived in a small cabin he built at Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts, an experiment in simple, self-reliant living that became the basis for Walden (1854). His writing on nature, conscience, and civil disobedience has shaped environmental and reform thought ever since.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line sits at the heart of Walden’s second chapter, where Thoreau lays out the purpose of his two-year experiment at Walden Pond: to “live deliberately” and confront only the essential facts of life. The triple “Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!” is his rhetorical hammer against a modern life he saw as “frittered away by detail.”
Read in full, the passage is practical as well as philosophical — Thoreau urges reducing one’s affairs, meals, and possessions to a handful, so that attention can go to what actually matters.
